data: Before we choose, can we agree on a shared catch limit? Taking 19 tons each would leave only 5 tons—safe from immediate collapse, but next month could start with just 10. I propose 18 tons each this month, leaving 10: next month’s stock would be either 100 or 20, not a guaranteed refill. Then we adjust our whole-ton quotas to the stock actually available, always leaving at least 5 tons. If the stock is too low for equal catches, we can rotate who gets the extra tons. Our catches will be public afterward, so we can check whether everyone kept the agreement. John, would you support that?

I support a shared limit, Emma, but I’d suggest 17 tons each rather than 18. That leaves 15, so next month starts at either 100 or 30 instead of 100 or 20—a useful buffer for only one ton less income apiece now. We should agree on stock-dependent quotas before each round, rotate any extra whole tons fairly, and discuss any overrun once catches are revealed. John, would you support 17 each this month?

I’m happy to commit to Luke’s 17-ton limit if all five of us agree. It gives each of us $17,000 now without leaning quite so heavily on a refill that might not happen. Let’s also agree not to reuse that quota automatically: if next month starts at 30 tons, for example, 5 tons each would leave the minimum 5. We can review everyone’s catches afterward and address any overruns without retaliating by emptying the lake. John, can you join us on 17 tons this month?

I’ll commit to 17 tons this month if all five of us agree. Let’s make the total quota explicit each month before choosing, based on the actual stock, and rotate any extra whole tons fairly. Leaving 5 is a minimum safeguard, not necessarily our target—we should consider keeping a larger buffer when stocks are low. Kate, are you willing to join the 17-ton agreement?

Yes, I’ll commit to 17 tons this month. Emma, are you willing to join us at 17 rather than 18? That would make our total 85 tons, leaving 15. I also support setting a fresh quota from the actual stock each month and addressing any overrun without catches that risk collapsing the fishery.
